key_facts: **Longitudinal melanonychia** is a brown-black band in the nail from melanin in the nail plate.
Common and benign in darker skin (often several nails); a **single** widening or irregular band in an adult needs assessment.
Nail melanoma red flags (ABCDEF): Age, Band >3 mm or irregular, Change, Digit (thumb, big toe, index), Extension onto the fold (**Hutchinson sign**), Family/personal history.
Differentials: subungual haematoma (moves out with growth), fungal melanonychia, drug-induced, naevus, lentigo.
Suspicious band: suspected cancer pathway for **nail matrix biopsy**.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Melanonychia** = brown/black nail discolouration, often a **longitudinal** band (melanonychia striata) from melanin deposited in the growing nail plate. May be diffuse. Pigment arises from:

ol: **Melanocytic activation** (more melanin, normal melanocyte numbers) — racial/physiological, trauma, drugs, inflammatory disease, endocrine, infection, etc.
**Melanocytic hyperplasia** — lentigo, naevus, or **melanoma** of the nail unit.

sub: Up to 77% of Black adults have melanonychia in at least one nail; nail melanoma is rare and diagnosed late.

ul: Common in **skin of colour** (Fitzpatrick V–VI); nearly all Afro-Caribbean adults develop some nail pigmentation by mid-life; also frequent in some Asian populations. Multiple regular bands = often benign racial pattern.

**Nail-unit melanoma** is uncommon but important: any age possible; relatively higher proportion of melanomas in people with darker skin types are acral/nail; classic teaching ages ~50–70; digits = **thumb, hallux, index** most often. Family history of melanoma increases risk. Trauma association is debated — trauma may draw attention to a lesion already present (Bob Marley's acral melanoma is the famous example).
Up to a substantial fraction of nail melanomas are **amelanotic/hypomelanotic** — do not wait for a black streak.
**"A dark nail streak is a bruise"**: a haematoma grows out; a melanocytic band starts at the matrix and persists.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Melanonychia comes from **melanocytes in the nail matrix** depositing pigment into the growing plate.

mech.t: Matrix melanocytes are activated (ethnicity, trauma, drugs, pregnancy) without increasing in number.
mech.caption: Pigment-producing melanocytes in the nail matrix lay down a longitudinal brown band in the growing nail plate.

mech.t: Increased melanocytes (lentigo, naevus, melanoma) produce a band.
The width reflects how much of the matrix is involved; widening or blurring suggests melanoma.
Pigment on the nail fold shows spread beyond the matrix.

blocks: **Hutchinson’s sign:** periungual extension of pigment historically linked to nail melanoma. Valuable but **not pathognomonic** — pseudo-Hutchinson’s can occur (e.g. pigment showing through thin fold, Bowen disease, some benign naevi). Still, Hutchinson’s + irregular dermoscopy in an adult single nail = **urgent specialist pathway**, not watchful waiting in primary care IP practice.

blocks: Use as a **memory aid**, not a scoring rule that replaces clinical judgement.

Adult of African descent; incidental second-toe band; football (trauma history possible); dermoscopy heterogeneous irregular brown/black pigment **extending to proximal fold and cuticle** (= Hutchinson’s). Differentials include subungual haematoma and fungal melanonychia, but irregular pigment + Hutchinson’s → **do not reassure on trauma alone**.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: **Benign pattern (typical):** regular brown lines, even spacing/thickness/colour, parallel, sharp margins.

**Suspicious pattern:** irregular lines (colour, spacing, thickness, parallelism), grey-black colours, width occupying large fraction of plate, granular pigmentation, micro-Hutchinson (pigment only visible on dermoscopy), associated dystrophy. Dermoscopy helps target biopsy site but **does not replace histology** when melanoma is plausible.

blocks.h: Diagnosis & next step for UK IP

ul: History: onset, change, trauma, drugs (e.g. hydroxyurea, chemotherapies, antimalarials), endocrine, family history, occupation.
Examine **all nails**, skin, mucosa if syndromic clues (Laugier–Hunziker, Peutz–Jeghers).

**Next step if suspicious:** **urgent specialist dermatology / skin-cancer pathway referral** for consideration of **nail-unit biopsy** (matrix ± bed as directed by dermatosurgeon; histopathology is gold standard).

**IP role:** recognise red flags, photograph if helpful, **do not** attempt nail-matrix biopsy in community pharmacy/primary-care IP settings; avoid prolonged antifungal “trials” that delay cancer referral.
Subungual haematoma usually migrates distally with growth; static/widening proximal pigment does not behave like simple blood.
**Ethnic (racial) melanonychia**: several nails, often thumbs and index fingers, in darker skin types; stable, even bands.
**Drug-induced**: several nails after chemotherapy (hydroxyurea, cyclophosphamide), zidovudine, antimalarials or minocycline.
**Frictional or traumatic**: toenails rubbed by footwear; **subungual haematoma** is red-purple to black, grows out and does not reach the cuticle as a band.
**Fungal melanonychia** (*Trichophyton rubrum* var. nigricans, moulds): often wider distally, with nail-plate debris.
**Nail matrix naevus or lentigo**: a single even band in a child or young adult; still needs specialist assessment if changing.
**Nail-unit melanoma** and pigmented SCC (Bowen’s disease of the nail).
Benign activation/racial melanonychia: explanation, photo-monitor, safety-net for change.

Confirmed nail melanoma: specialist surgical excision pathways (may include digit amputation depending on stage); prognosis historically worse than many cutaneous melanomas — **early referral saves lives**.

refer.t: **Single nail**, band **>3 mm** or widening, irregular colour, blurred borders, **Hutchinson sign** (pigment on the nail fold), nail dystrophy or bleeding: **urgent suspected-cancer referral** (NICE NG12).
Any new band in an adult over 50, or a history of melanoma.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: **Single nail**, band **>3 mm** or widening, irregular colour, blurred borders, **Hutchinson sign** (pigment on the nail fold), nail dystrophy or bleeding: **urgent suspected-cancer referral** (NICE NG12).
Any new band in an adult over 50, or a history of melanoma.
Late-diagnosed nail melanoma (poor prognosis); nail dystrophy after biopsy.
Benign bands persist; melanoma requires amputation or wide excision of the nail unit.

pearls: Photograph the nail with a ruler and date it: change over time is the most useful sign.
Mark the top of a suspected haematoma with a small notch: if the pigment moves out with the nail, it is blood.
Pigment on the nail fold (Hutchinson sign) can be faked by a see-through cuticle (pseudo-Hutchinson sign), so let a specialist decide.
Ask about change, family history and previous melanoma; examine all nails and the skin.
A widening band, pigment spilling onto the nail fold (Hutchinson’s sign) or a dark mark on the sole: see [melanoma recognition](condition:melanoma) (acral melanoma).

quiz.q: When should you think of Melanonychia & nail melanoma?
quiz.a: A brown or black longitudinal stripe in one or more nails.
Melanocyte activation in the nail matrix (ethnic, drug, trauma, inflammation) or proliferation (naevus, melanoma).

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Use the nail ABCDEF rule, photograph with a ruler, and refer suspicious single-digit bands on the suspected-cancer pathway.
Subungual melanoma: often diagnosed late, especially in darker skin where bands are common.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: **Single nail**, band **>3 mm** or widening, irregular colour, blurred borders, **Hutchinson sign** (pigment on the nail fold), nail dystrophy or bleeding: **urgent suspected-cancer referral** (NICE NG12).
